query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, a dynamic amorphization mechanism that forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near‐surface layer governs hardness and strength. Below a critical grain size, this amorphous layer increases resistance to plastic deformation via grain boundary‐mediated processes, giving rise to inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) in a coarse-grained condition without significant near-surface amorphization.
generation.intervention: Process the alloy to refine the grain structure—using methods such as severe plastic deformation and controlled annealing under inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions—to achieve grain sizes below the critical threshold that facilitates dynamic amorphization.
generation.conditions: All samples must have identical alloy compositions and be tested in inert environments (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) to avoid oxidation effects. The only variable is the grain size and associated near-surface microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized near-surface layer with high-angle grain boundaries, which modifies shear strength and hardness.
generation.mechanism: As the grain size decreases past a critical value, dynamic amorphization occurs at the surface, forming a structure that impedes dislocation motion and enhances material strength. This near-surface layer, through its unique grain boundary characteristics, underpins the observed inversion in the Hall-Petch trend.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained samples, ultrafine-grained samples will display increased hardness and tensile strength. A strong correlation between reduced grain size (and the emergence of the amorphized layer) and enhanced mechanical properties is expected, up to a limit defined by grain boundary stability.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained high entropy alloy samples lacking the dynamically formed near-surface amorphous layer, exhibiting lower hardness and strength.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under inert conditions (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) and for high-entropy alloys with similar compositions to CoCrFeMnNi. It may not apply in oxidizing environments or for alloys where the intrinsic grain boundary energies or compositions preclude dynamic amorphization.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical grain size for triggering dynamic amorphization and the universality of this behavior across various high-entropy alloy compositions remain undetermined. Variations in processing kinetics and alloy chemistry might also affect the formation and stability of the amorphous layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high entropy alloy samples under identical processing conditions except for the treatment of the near-surface region. The first set should be processed to induce ultrafine grain formation and dynamic amorphization (maintaining the ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer). The second set should undergo a post-deformation heat treatment designed to disrupt or coarsen the near-surface amorphous layer. Test both sets in an inert environment.
measurements: Grain size and microstructure via STEM/TEM to verify the presence or absence of the near-surface ultra-nanocrystalline layer
XRD or other surface phase analyses to characterize the crystallinity/amorphous nature of the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the set with the intact near-surface amorphous layer does not exhibit significantly higher hardness and strength compared to the group where this layer is disrupted, or if inverse Hall-Petch behavior is not observed despite the expected microstructural differences, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
